title: “THOSE WHO WANT TO GET RICH FALL INTO TEMPTATION” — THE BIBLE VERSE WE KEEP CROPPING OUT OF OUR CHRISTIAN SUCCESS STORIES
paragraphs: “THOSE WHO WANT TO GET RICH FALL INTO TEMPTATION” — THE BIBLE VERSE WE KEEP CROPPING OUT OF OUR CHRISTIAN SUCCESS STORIES

We celebrate the promotion, the new house, the overflowing bank account, and the testimony of financial breakthrough. But what if the greatest danger isn't having too little money… but slowly becoming someone who can no longer recognize Jesus without it?
There is a frightening possibility that almost nobody wants to discuss in a Christian success testimony.
You can finally get everything you prayed for… and slowly lose the heart that once prayed.
You can build the business, buy the house, pay off the debts, wear the expensive clothes, and stand before a congregation telling everyone how good God has been.
And God may indeed have been good to you.
But somewhere between the first answered prayer and the next financial milestone, something can quietly change.
You stop asking, “Lord, what do You want me to do?”
And start asking, “Lord, how can You help me get more?”
You still attend church. You still quote Scripture. You still thank God publicly.
But privately, your peace now depends on numbers.
Your happiness rises and falls with your income.
Your sense of worth depends on what you can afford.
And the Jesus who once meant everything to you has slowly become Someone you consult when your plans need divine approval.
That is not always what losing faith looks like.
Sometimes losing your first love looks like becoming successful enough that you no longer notice how far your heart has wandered.
And before you dismiss this as another article attacking prosperity, listen carefully.
The Bible does not condemn having money. It warns us about what happens when money begins having us.
There is a difference.
A difference that can determine whether your success becomes an instrument of worship or an altar where your soul is slowly sacrificed.
And the apostle Paul gave us a warning so uncomfortable that it rarely fits beneath a photograph of a luxury car captioned, “God did it.”
In 1 Timothy 6:9, Scripture says:
“But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Not merely those who steal to become rich.
Not merely those who exploit others.
Not merely those who worship idols openly.
Those who want to be rich.
The Greek text begins:
οἱ δὲ βουλόμενοι πλουτεῖν
hoi de boulomenoi ploutein
“But those who desire to be rich…”
The verb βούλομαι (boulomai) speaks of wanting, wishing, or intending. And πλουτεῖν (ploutein) means to be rich or to become wealthy.
Paul is addressing people whose desire is directed toward becoming rich.
He is not declaring that every financially successful person is wicked. He is exposing the spiritual danger of making wealth the object of our pursuit.
The verse continues:
ἐμπίπτουσιν εἰς πειρασμὸν καὶ παγίδα
empiptousin eis peirasmon kai pagida
“They fall into temptation and a snare.”
The Greek word παγίδα (pagida) means a trap or snare.
Think about that.
A trap does not usually announce itself as a trap.
It presents something desirable.
Something worth chasing.
Something that appears to promise relief.
And by the time the victim understands what has happened, the trap has already tightened.
Paul continues by describing harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction.
The language is severe because the danger is severe.
And perhaps the most disturbing part is this:
The person caught in the trap may still believe they are simply pursuing God's blessings.
Imagine a man sitting in his car outside his workplace.
He has been there for twenty minutes.
The engine is off.
His hands are gripping the steering wheel.
His phone is filled with overdue payment reminders.
His children need school supplies. His wife has been stretching the grocery budget. His parents need help with medication.
He whispers something he has prayed a hundred times.
“Lord, I just want to make enough so my family won't suffer anymore.”
There is nothing shameful about that prayer.
There is nothing sinful about working hard to provide for people you love.
In fact, Scripture speaks seriously about caring for one's household (1 Timothy 5:8).
And if you have ever watched someone you love struggle because there was not enough money, you understand why financial security can feel like more than a desire.
It can feel like rescue.
You remember the embarrassment of borrowing.
The fear of opening bills.
The silent calculations at the supermarket.
The nights you pretended you weren't hungry so your children could have another serving.
You remember promising yourself that one day, if God gave you the opportunity, your family would never experience that humiliation again.
And perhaps God did open a door.
You found a better job.
Your small business started growing.
You learned new skills.
You worked when everyone else was sleeping.
Slowly, life became easier.
Then one day, you looked around and realized you were no longer struggling to survive.
But something unexpected happened.
Enough stopped feeling like enough.
The house you once prayed for began feeling too small.
The salary that once brought you to tears of gratitude became disappointing.
The people you once admired for their kindness began looking less impressive than people who earned more than you.
And without making a conscious decision, you moved the finish line.
Again.
And again.
And again.
You told yourself, “Just a little more, and I'll finally rest.”
But rest never came.
Because the heart that believes money will finally make it secure will always find another reason to be afraid.
This is where the Gospel confronts us with a question that cannot be answered by showing our bank statements.
When did providing for your family become proving your worth?
When did responsible ambition become endless comparison?
When did gratitude become entitlement?
When did God's provision stop being something to steward and become something you could never have enough of?
Paul understood this danger.
But notice what he wrote immediately before the warning.
In 1 Timothy 6:6, he said:
“But godliness with contentment is great gain.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “contentment” is αὐτάρκεια (autarkeia), a word associated with sufficiency or contentment.
Paul is not saying Christians should abandon work, ignore responsibilities, or romanticize poverty.
He is telling us that true spiritual gain is not measured by how much we accumulate.
It is found in a life shaped by godliness and contentment.
And then he reminds us of a truth that makes every billionaire and every struggling laborer equal before eternity:
“For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.” (1 Timothy 6:7, KJV)
Nothing.
Not your land titles.
Not your investments.
Not your luxury watches.
Not your online followers.
Not the business you built.
Not even the home you spent thirty years paying for.
One day, someone else will hold the keys.
Someone else will occupy your office.
Someone else will decide what happens to the possessions you guarded so carefully.
And the only question that will ultimately matter is not how much you managed to keep.
It is whether you belonged to Jesus Christ.
That should make us think.
Because we live in a generation where even Christian success can become a performance.
We post the new car and call it favor.
We post the expensive vacation and call it breakthrough.
We post the business achievement and call it divine elevation.
And sometimes those things truly are blessings received with sincere thanksgiving.
There is nothing inherently wrong with celebrating honest provision.
But we must be careful not to teach people that material increase is the clearest evidence of God's approval.
Because somewhere, a faithful Christian mother is praying over a nearly empty refrigerator.
Somewhere, a godly father has been unemployed for months despite sending applications every day.
Somewhere, a believer who loves Jesus deeply is battling an illness that has consumed the family's savings.
Somewhere, a pastor is serving a small congregation without recognition or financial comfort.
Are they less blessed?
Does their poverty mean they lack faith?
Does their suffering mean God has forgotten them?
Absolutely not.
And we must never preach a version of Christianity that makes struggling believers feel spiritually inferior because they cannot afford the lifestyle of the people holding the microphone.
Jesus did not measure the widow's devotion by the size of her offering.
In Mark 12:41–44, He saw a poor widow place two small coins into the temple treasury.
Others contributed much larger amounts.
But Jesus drew His disciples' attention to her.
Why?
Because He saw something beyond the amount.
He saw sacrifice.
He saw the heart.

The passage does not give religious leaders permission to pressure vulnerable people into giving away what they need to survive. It calls our attention to a widow whom Jesus noticed, while the surrounding context also warns about religious figures who exploit widows.
God sees what human applause often overlooks.
And sometimes the believer with almost nothing understands generosity more deeply than the person who gives large amounts without ever feeling the cost.
Now consider another man.
He approached Jesus with what appeared to be a sincere spiritual question.
He wanted eternal life.
He had kept the commandments, at least as he understood them.
He was respectable.
Disciplined.
Religious.
And wealthy.
In Mark 10:21, Scripture records something extraordinary.
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him…” (KJV)
Do not miss those words.
Jesus loved him.
Before confronting his attachment to wealth, Jesus loved him.
Before revealing what held his heart captive, Jesus loved him.
The confrontation was not an expression of hatred.
It was love refusing to leave a man deceived.
Jesus told him to sell what he possessed, give to the poor, and follow Him.
And the man walked away grieving because he had great possessions.
Think about the tragedy.
He stood face-to-face with the One who could give him eternal life.
The One through whom all things were made.
The One who would surrender His own life for sinners.
And he walked away because he could not release his wealth.
He had possessions.
But his possessions had him.
And the most heartbreaking part is that Jesus did not stop loving him when he walked away.
The passage does not tell us what ultimately happened to that man.
It leaves us standing in the uncomfortable silence of his decision.
What would you have done?
Not what you would say in church.
What would you actually do if following Jesus threatened the thing that made you feel secure?
Your salary?
Your reputation?
Your lifestyle?
Your business relationships?
Your ambition to become somebody important?
Would you still follow Him?
Or would you walk away sorrowful, carrying everything you owned while leaving behind the One your soul needed most?
There is another passage that should trouble anyone who confuses wealth with spiritual safety.
Jesus told a parable about a rich man whose land produced an abundant harvest.
The man had so much that he decided to tear down his barns and build larger ones.
He planned to store his goods and enjoy many years of ease.
But God said to him:
“Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee…” (Luke 12:20, KJV)
The issue was not that the land produced a good harvest.
The issue was the man's self-centered confidence.
He spoke repeatedly about his crops, his barns, his goods, and his future.
But his plans revealed no dependence on God and no concern for anyone beyond himself.
He had prepared for many years of living.
He had not prepared to meet his Maker.
And Jesus concluded with a warning against storing up treasure for oneself without being rich toward God.
Imagine spending your whole life building a future you never get to enter.
Imagine finally reaching the income you always wanted, only to discover that your children barely know you.
Imagine owning a beautiful house where nobody feels loved.
Imagine being admired by thousands of strangers while the people closest to you quietly grieve the person you have become.
Imagine having enough money to purchase almost anything you desire but being unable to purchase back the years you spent chasing it.
That is not success.
That is a tragedy wearing expensive clothes.
And yet, the Bible does not tell every wealthy believer to abandon all possessions.
In 1 Timothy 6:17–19, Paul gives specific instructions to Christians who are rich in this present world.
He does not tell them that their wealth automatically makes them enemies of God.
He tells them not to be arrogant.
Not to place their hope in uncertain riches.
But to place their hope in God, who richly provides things for our enjoyment.
Then he commands them to do good, to be rich in good works, generous, and willing to share.
That is biblical stewardship.
Not shame over possessing resources.
Not pride in possessing resources.
But humility, gratitude, generosity, and obedience.
Abraham had wealth.
Job possessed great resources.
Joseph of Arimathea was a rich man who honored Jesus.
Lydia, a merchant of purple cloth, opened her home in service to the early church.
Their stories do not establish a promise that every faithful Christian will become financially wealthy.
They demonstrate that possessions can be placed under God's authority.
The question is never simply, “How much do you have?”
The deeper question is, “Who rules your heart?”
Because money is a powerful servant.
But a cruel master.
And Jesus said something that leaves no room for negotiation.
“Ye cannot serve God and mammon.” (Matthew 6:24, KJV)
The word μαμωνᾷ (mamōna) refers to wealth or riches.
Jesus was not saying that earning money is incompatible with serving God.
He was saying that wealth cannot become our rival master.
You can use money while serving Christ.
You cannot serve money while pretending Christ still occupies the throne.
And that distinction becomes painfully clear when obedience begins to cost you something.
When honesty threatens a profitable contract.
When integrity means refusing a business opportunity.
When generosity interrupts a personal luxury.
When keeping the Sabbath or setting aside time for worship challenges your schedule.
When a struggling employee needs compassion more than your company needs another percentage point of profit.
When your family needs your presence more than they need another expensive gift.
Those moments reveal what we actually worship.
Not the inspirational captions.
Not the worship music playing in our cars.
Not the Bible verses hanging in our offices.
Our decisions.
Our sacrifices.
Our priorities.
The things we refuse to surrender.
And perhaps someone reading this is beginning to feel uncomfortable.
You worked hard.
You sacrificed.
You endured years of financial struggle.
You believe God helped you reach where you are today.
And now this article seems to be questioning something you once considered a blessing.
Please understand.
The goal is not to make you feel guilty for God's provision.
The goal is to protect you from turning His provision into a substitute for His presence.
There is no holiness in pretending money does not matter when your children need food.
There is no virtue in neglecting bills or refusing honest opportunities.
And there is no biblical command requiring every Christian to remain poor.
But there is also no promise that becoming rich will heal the deepest wounds in your soul.
Some people pursue wealth because they are greedy.
Others pursue it because they are terrified.
Terrified of being helpless again.
Terrified of disappointing their families.
Terrified of being looked down upon.
Terrified of becoming the person everyone forgets.
And sometimes the hunger for more money is covering a wound that began long before the first paycheck.
Maybe you grew up watching your parents argue about bills.
Maybe you were humiliated because your clothes were old.
Maybe someone told you that you would never amount to anything.
Maybe you were abandoned when you had nothing.
So you made a private promise.
“One day, I'll become so successful that nobody will ever make me feel small again.”
And for years, that promise became your fuel.
But now you are exhausted.
Because no amount of money can permanently silence a voice that has convinced you that you are worthless without achievement.
Only the truth of who you are before God can begin to confront that lie.
And the Gospel speaks directly into that wound.
Jesus did not come to offer you a more impressive social status.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He came for the proud and the ashamed.
The wealthy and the struggling.
The religious and the rebellious.
The people who had wasted their lives chasing pleasure and the people who had spent their lives trying to earn approval.
He came because our deepest problem was never simply a shortage of resources.
It was sin.
Separation from God.
Hearts that continually exchange the Creator for created things.
And at the cross, Jesus Christ gave Himself for sinners who could never purchase their own redemption.
The apostle Peter wrote:
“Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold…” (1 Peter 1:18, KJV)
And then he tells us how redemption comes.
“But with the precious blood of Christ…” (1 Peter 1:19, KJV)
Not silver.
Not gold.
Not investments.
Not achievements.
Not charitable donations.
Not church contributions.
The precious blood of Christ.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
Your forgiveness cannot be bought.
Your standing before God cannot be improved by the amount you earn or donate.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of works, so that no one can boast.
And that means the person who owns ten companies and the person who cannot afford tomorrow's groceries must come to God through the same Savior.
Jesus Christ.
No premium entrance.
No financial qualification.
No special treatment for the wealthy.
At the foot of the cross, human boasting dies.
And grace begins.
This is why the Gospel is so radically different from the world's definition of success.
The world says, “Become important enough that people will finally recognize your value.”
Jesus says that even while we were sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).
The world says, “Accumulate enough that you will never need anyone.”
Jesus teaches us to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11).
The world says, “Protect everything you own.”
Jesus says to seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness (Matthew 6:33).
The world says, “Your possessions prove who you are.”
Jesus warns that a person's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions (Luke 12:15).
And perhaps that is the warning our Christian success culture needs to hear again.
Not every open door is an invitation to pursue wealth without restraint.
Not every financial increase proves spiritual maturity.
Not every luxury is a sin.
Not every poor person is righteous.
Not every wealthy person is greedy.
And not every opportunity that promises more money deserves the sacrifice it demands.
We need discernment.
We need contentment.
We need generosity.
We need repentance when ambition becomes an idol.
We need the courage to celebrate God's provision without turning financial success into the standard by which we judge other believers.
And above all, we need Jesus.
Consider Zacchaeus.
He was a wealthy chief tax collector, a man associated with a system that could be used to exploit others.
When Jesus entered his life, something changed.
Zacchaeus stood and declared that he would give half of his possessions to the poor and repay fourfold anyone he had defrauded.
Jesus responded:
“This day is salvation come to this house…” (Luke 19:9, KJV)
Notice the transformation.
Zacchaeus did not purchase salvation through generosity.
His changed relationship with money revealed the fruit of an encounter with Jesus.
The man who had once accumulated wealth through a compromised life began using his possessions to make things right.
That is repentance becoming visible.
That is grace producing transformation.
That is what happens when Jesus rewrites a story.
The Gospel does not merely teach us how to manage money.
It transforms what we love.
And when our love changes, our relationship with money changes too.
We can work diligently without worshiping achievement.
We can build businesses without exploiting people.
We can save responsibly without placing our ultimate hope in savings.
We can enjoy God's gifts without forgetting the Giver.
We can give generously without expecting God to repay us with guaranteed financial returns.
We can celebrate success without making those who struggle feel forgotten.
And we can endure seasons of scarcity without believing that God has abandoned us.
Because the greatest blessing of the Christian life is not becoming rich.
It is belonging to Christ.
Paul knew what it meant to live with both abundance and need.
In Philippians 4:12–13, he described learning to live in humble circumstances and in prosperity, to be full and to be hungry.
His strength was not a formula for unlimited financial achievement.
It was the sufficiency of Christ in changing circumstances.
That is a very different message from the idea that faith guarantees material prosperity.
And it is a message our souls desperately need.
Because there may come a day when the business fails.
When the economy changes.
When the savings disappear.
When the diagnosis arrives.
When the job you thought was secure suddenly ends.
And if your confidence has been built entirely upon financial stability, everything inside you may begin to collapse.
But if your hope is anchored in Jesus Christ, loss does not have the final word.
You may grieve.
You may struggle.
You may need help.
You may face painful uncertainty.
Faith does not make those experiences unreal.
But your identity does not disappear with your income.
Your worth does not vanish with your possessions.
And the Savior who redeemed you when you had nothing does not cease to be faithful when you lose what you once had.
Some of you are reading this with tears you did not expect.
Not because you hate money.
Not because you regret working hard.
But because you recognize how tired your soul has become.
You have spent so many years trying to become financially secure that you cannot remember the last time you felt spiritually at rest.
You pray, but your mind keeps returning to your financial goals.
You worship, but comparison keeps stealing your joy.
You give, but part of you keeps calculating what you might receive in return.
You have become so accustomed to measuring progress through achievement that you struggle to recognize the quiet work God is doing in your character.
And maybe today, the Holy Spirit is confronting something you have avoided naming.
Your ambition has become an idol.
Not necessarily because you have money.
But because you have begun asking money to give you what only God can provide.
Identity.
Security.
Peace.
Meaning.
A reason to believe your life matters.
And if that is you, the answer is not despair.
It is repentance.
Turn back to Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.

“Lord, I have been afraid of not having enough. I have compared myself to others. I have allowed success to become more important than obedience. I have chased things that cannot satisfy my soul. Forgive me. Teach me to work faithfully without worshiping wealth. Teach me to receive with gratitude, to give with joy, and to trust You whether I have much or little.”
You do not need an impressive speech.
You need an honest heart.
And if you have never truly trusted Christ, do not mistake religious activity for reconciliation with God.
Turn from sin and trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
He died for sins and rose again.
His grace is not a reward for people who have finally become successful enough.
It is God's gift to sinners who cannot save themselves.
And that includes you.
Perhaps your scandal was not something the world could easily see.
Perhaps it was not adultery, addiction, or public disgrace.
Perhaps it was the quiet scandal of a heart that gradually made success its god.
Perhaps nobody noticed.
You were still respected.
Still productive.
Still admired.
Still attending church.
But Jesus knew.
And He was not calling you to surrender because He wanted to rob you of joy.
He was calling you away from a master that could never love you back.
Money cannot forgive your sins.
Money cannot resurrect the dead.
Money cannot cleanse your conscience.
Money cannot promise eternal life.
Money cannot hold you through death.
But Jesus can save completely those who come to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25).
And when He restores a heart, even the way that heart handles money begins to change.
So if this article has exposed something uncomfortable, do not rush past it.
Sit with the question.
If God never made you wealthy, would Jesus still be enough for you?
Not enough to erase every difficulty.
Not enough to make bills irrelevant.
But enough to remain worthy of your worship, trust, and obedience.
Would you still love Him?
Would you still follow Him?
Would you still call Him good?
That question is not intended to condemn people who are struggling to survive.
It is intended to uncover what occupies the throne of our hearts.
And it is a question worth answering before success makes it easier to avoid.
You can write, “Jesus, teach me to be content.”
Or, if you are fighting to trust God in financial hardship, comment, “Pray for me. I'm still trusting Jesus.”
You do not have to disclose your income, your debts, or any private details. Even a few honest words may encourage another believer who thought they were fighting this battle alone.
And if you have experienced the freedom of no longer measuring your worth by your possessions, share your testimony. Someone needs to know that contentment in Christ is possible.
There is also something deeply practical you can do.
Not to shame people who are prospering.
Not to attack Christians who have been blessed with financial resources.
But to remind your friends and family that the Gospel is greater than any prosperity message that reduces God's goodness to material increase.
Because our mission is not to teach people how to appear spiritually successful.
Our mission is to point people to the Savior who transforms sinners by grace.
And if this message has helped you, I want to invite you to become part of the continuing work of Gospel Warrior.

We are building a place where biblical truth is not reserved for those who can afford it, where people wrestling with guilt, fear, spiritual exhaustion, temptation, and questions about faith can encounter Scripture-centered encouragement and be directed back to Jesus Christ.
We want those resources to remain accessible.
We want more people to encounter faithful Christian teaching.
That work requires time, resources, and faithful support.
And it should never replace the financial responsibilities you already have toward your family or the commitments you have made to your local church.
But it can be a voluntary, recurring expression of generosity toward Gospel-centered digital ministry, much like other freewill offerings given to support Christian work.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14), while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not reluctant or forced.
Not pressure.
Not fear.
But partnership.
An opportunity to help sustain and expand a ministry you believe is serving others.
If you have been asking how you can use a portion of God's provision to glorify Him, supporting faithful Gospel work is one meaningful possibility among many.
These are simply expressions of appreciation. They are not the reason we follow Jesus, and they are not the measure of anyone's faithfulness.
You are welcome here.
The free resources are still for you.
The Gospel is still for you.
Your encouragement and participation matter.
No one needs to prove their love for Jesus by sending money to a particular ministry.
What matters is a heart increasingly surrendered to Him.
And perhaps that is the most fitting place to end an article about wealth.
Because after everything we have said about money, ambition, generosity, and contentment, the final invitation is not to become a more impressive donor.
It is to become a more faithful disciple.
To remember that every resource entrusted to us is temporary.
To remember that our greatest treasure cannot be purchased.
To remember that Jesus is not merely the One who can bless our plans.
He is Lord.
And when the world tells us that we need more to finally become somebody, we can remember that the Son of God gave Himself to redeem people who could never afford their own salvation.
One day, your financial achievements will belong to history.
The photographs will fade.
The applause will stop.
The possessions will pass into other hands.
But the grace of God in Jesus Christ is not temporary.
And the life He gives cannot be measured by an account balance.
So work hard.
Provide faithfully.
Plan wisely.
Give generously.
Enjoy God's provision with thanksgiving.
But do not lose your soul chasing what you cannot carry into eternity.
Because the richest person in the room is not necessarily the one who owns the most.
And the poorest person in the room is not necessarily the one who has the least.
The question is whether we have Christ.
And whether Christ has our hearts.
You can spend your entire life becoming rich enough to own the world, only to discover that the one treasure you could never afford was already offered to you freely at the cross.
